explain.say: After more than a century of civil war, Tokugawa Ieyasu won the battle of Sekigahara in 1600. His family then kept Japan at peace for about 250 years, one of the longest peaceful eras of any large country. Look at the timeline of how they did it.

explain.say: Look at 1635: alternate attendance, sankin-kōtai. Every regional lord, a daimyo, had to live in Edo every other year and leave his family there when he went home. The long processions cost a fortune. Why would that keep lords from rebelling?

explain.say: Now 1639 and 1641. Fearing Christianity and foreign meddling, the shogunate banned Portuguese ships and confined Dutch traders to Dejima, a small artificial island at Nagasaki. Look at the map: Dutch ships came from Batavia, today's Jakarta. Japan seemed closed. But was it?

draw.label: Edo, Kyoto and the Dutch route

explain.say: See the network. Historians now speak of four gates: Nagasaki for Dutch and Chinese traders, Tsushima for Korea, Satsuma for the Ryukyu kingdom, and Matsumae for the Ainu in the north. The word sakoku, locked country, was only coined in 1801. Which gate surprises you most?

Inside, Edo grew to about a million people, with booming books, kabuki theatre and woodblock prints. In 1853 American warships under Perry forced Japan to open, and the shogunate fell in 1868. Superb work. Exam tip: write managed contact rather than isolation, and cite Ronald Toby.

faq.a: Alternate attendance, formalised in 1635: daimyo had to spend every other year in Edo and leave their wives and heirs there. It kept lords under watch and drained their wealth, while boosting roads and Edo's economy.

Not fully. After 1639 Portuguese ships were banned and Japanese could not travel abroad, but trade and diplomacy continued through four gates: Nagasaki, Tsushima, Satsuma and Matsumae. Historians call it managed contact.

A small artificial island in Nagasaki harbour where Dutch East India Company traders were confined from 1641 to 1859. Through it came goods, news and Western learning, known as rangaku, Dutch studies.

faq.q: How did the Tokugawa keep peace for 250 years?
faq.a: By balancing control and local rule: daimyo kept their domains but faced alternate attendance, limits on castles and marriages, a fixed status order, careful control of foreign contact and a ban on Christianity.

faq.q: Who were the four gates of Tokugawa Japan?
faq.a: Nagasaki, where Dutch and Chinese traders came; Tsushima, which handled Korea; Satsuma, which controlled trade with the Ryukyu kingdom; and Matsumae, which traded with the Ainu people of Hokkaido.
